guide.summary: Forgejo documents OAuth2 Authorization Code with PKCE for user tokens on each customer instance. OAuth2 scopes are not implemented, so the token is unscoped and acts as the connected user, with administrative rights for third-party apps; the read-only boundary must be enforced by the app.

findings.title: Forgejo OAuth2 provider: Authorization Code with PKCE; tokens are unscoped and act as the user
findings.detail: Forgejo acts as an OAuth2 provider with user consent and supports the Authorization Code Grant with PKCE. OAuth2 scopes are not implemented and tokens can execute any action on behalf of the user. Third-party applications obtaining a token for a user via an application have administrative rights, so the app must limit itself to read-only calls.
findings.appliesWhen: Customer connects an individual account on their own Forgejo instance using OAuth

evidence.quote: OAuth2 provider Forgejo supports acting as an OAuth2 provider to allow third party applications to access its resources with the user’s consent.
Supported OAuth2 Grants At the moment, Forgejo only supports the Authorization Code Grant standard with additional support for the following extensions:
Note Third-party applications obtaining a token for a user via such an application will have administrative rights.

findings.title: Register an OAuth2 application on the customer's Forgejo instance before testing
findings.detail: Any user can register an OAuth2 application on the instance's user settings applications page. Registration issues the client ID and secret used for the token exchange, and the redirect URI must match. Public clients must use PKCE and a loopback redirect where applicable.
findings.appliesWhen: Before the first test against each customer instance

evidence.quote: It is possible for any user to manually register a new OAuth2 application on the /user/settings/applications page for the purpose of using Git credential helpers different from the pre-registered ones.
